name: Principles of Food Preservation

objectives.text: Identify signs that food has spoiled, such as mold growth, off odors, sliminess, and changes in color or texture
Identify methods used to keep food from spoiling, such as refrigerating, freezing, drying, and canning
Explain that microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts, and molds cause much food spoilage and need food, water, and warmth to grow
Describe how canning, freezing, and drying each slow down food spoilage
Describe how enzymes and oxygen cause food to brown, soften, or turn rancid even when microorganisms are not present
Compare traditional preservation methods such as salting, smoking, and root cellaring with modern methods such as refrigeration and commercial canning
Explain how food preservation reduces food waste and helps farmers and families steward harvests across seasons
Explain how controlling moisture, temperature, acidity, and oxygen slows the growth of microorganisms in food
Apply the temperature danger zone to decide how long perishable foods may safely remain unrefrigerated

Identify the major food preservation methods, including thermal processing, refrigeration, freezing, dehydration, curing, irradiation, and chemical preservatives, and the spoilage factor each controls
Identify common preservation equipment such as pressure canners, dehydrators, vacuum sealers, and blast freezers and describe the function of each
Explain how water activity and pH determine which microorganisms can grow in a food and how preservation methods alter these factors
Analyze the advantages and limitations of canning, freezing, drying, and curing as preservation methods
Explain why low-acid foods require pressure canning to destroy Clostridium botulinum spores while high-acid foods can be safely processed in a boiling water bath
Analyze how common preservatives such as salt, sugar, nitrites, sorbates, and antioxidants inhibit spoilage and influence food chemistry
Apply a tested preservation procedure, such as dehydrating produce or canning tomatoes, in a lab or supervised agricultural experience project
Analyze the characteristics of food products to determine appropriate storage temperature, humidity, and duration
Analyze how combining several mild preservation hurdles can produce a safe, shelf-stable food product
Analyze how packaging methods such as vacuum sealing and modified atmosphere packaging extend shelf life and maintain desirable food qualities
Evaluate a preservation method's effectiveness at maintaining the nutritional and sensory quality of a food
Design a shelf-life study that measures changes in appearance, weight, microbial growth, or rancidity of a preserved product over time
Recommend preservation strategies for different foods based on their composition, intended market, and safety risks
Design a preservation process for a specific food product and justify the method chosen

changes: Kept all six existing objectives as real competencies, rewording the grade 3 and grade 7 items to broaden them (adding refrigeration and canning, and acidity and oxygen as spoilage factors). Added missing principles across the span: signs of spoilage, microorganisms as spoilage agents, enzymatic and oxidative spoilage, traditional versus modern methods, stewardship and food waste, the temperature danger zone, water activity and pH, botulism and low-acid canning, chemical preservatives, preservation equipment, storage conditions, hurdle technology, preservation packaging, shelf-life testing, and recommending strategies. Added hands-on application suited to labs and SAE. Left specific processing operations, dairy and meat curing detail, and fermentation to the sibling sub-topics. Assigned AFNR codes only to grade 9 to 12 objectives that directly teach them.
